newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Japan set to buy more Tanzanian coffee -- traders.
newsitem.headline: Japan set to buy more Tanzanian coffee -- traders.

text.p: Tanzanian coffee exports to Japan, averaging about 11,000 tonnes a year, are expected to rise with Japanese buyers showing increasing interest, a senior government official said on Sunday.

"Japan is the second largest importer of Tanzanian coffee and it's growing. But they're only interested in top quality coffee -- nothing else," said Edward Sannda, Managing Director of the state-run Tanzania Coffee Board TCB).
"If we continue to produce more top quality coffee I think this business will continue to grow."

Germany is the biggest coffee customer, buying 14,355 tonnes of mild washed arabicas, 439 tonnes of hard arabica and 1,732 tonnes of robusta in 1995. Other top buyers include the Netherlands, Belgium and France.
On Saturday, Sannda played host to a nine-man delegation from the All Japan Coffee Association (AJCA), the country's top industry body.

Promotion by the AJCA had been instrumental in raising Tanzanian coffee exports to Japan from an average of 5,000 tonnes a year between 1985 and 1992 to 11,000 tonnes average between 1993 and 1996, Sannda said.
Of 55,000 tonnes of coffee exported during the 1995/96 season, 19.8 percent of total exports was bought by the AJCA.

Speaking by telephone from Moshi, Tanzania's coffee centre, Sannda told Reuters that total Tanzanian coffee production for the 1997/98 season (starting in November) would be about 45,000 tonnes, reflecting the impact of drought which affected much of East Africa.
The 1996/97 crop is expected to total 41,000 tonnes worth $92 million.
The Japanese visitors were briefed in Moshi on key measures to boost production and quality of Tanzanian coffee by providing seedlings and finance for peasant farmers.
The TCB chief said plans were also under way to develop coffee production -- mainly arabica -- in Iringa and Morogoro, central Tanzania, and Kigoma and Mara, in the northwest.

Premium mild washed arabica, grown in the Kilimanjaro area of northern Tanzania, now represents half Tanzania's total arabica production which in turn accounts for about 75 percent of total coffee output.

Industry experts say Tanzania could substantially increase coffee production, which has declined in recent years because of poor plant husbandry, ageing trees, inter-cropping and erratic supply of inputs.
Coffee is sold at twice monthly auctions in Moshi, the headquarters of the TCB.
